lessons.title: Factorials and the product rule
lessons.summary: Simplify factorial ratios and justify the product rule.
lessons.objective: Simplify factorial ratios and justify the product rule.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to simplify factorial ratios and justify the product rule.
lessons.ideas:
Multiply the number of options at each stage. Filling a position removes one option from the remaining supply.

Expand only to the largest common factorial, then cancel it.

Cancel first, then solve the smaller polynomial equation.
lessons.method:
Write the choices for each position over a row of empty boxes. If all n positions are filled with distinct objects, the product is \(n!\).

Treat \(0!\) as one empty arrangement. For a longer numerator, step down one factor at a time.

Check that each resulting factorial argument is a non-negative integer. Use the context to choose a valid root.
mistakes: Adding the numbers of options misses the combinations of consecutive choices.
Cancel factors of the whole product. A factorial does not distribute over addition.
An algebraic root may lie outside the factorial domain.

examples.title: Use the product rule to arrange distinct objects
examples.question: Distinct posters are hung in a row. There are 7 objects. How many orders are possible with no restriction?
examples.solution:
There are 7 choices for the first place, 6 for the next, and so on down to one.

Multiply these choices to obtain \(7!\).

Answer: \(5040\).

examples.title: Cancel a factorial quotient
examples.question: Evaluate \(\frac{13!}{11!}\).
examples.solution:
The common factor is \(11!\). Cancel it.

Multiply the remaining factors: \(13\times12\).

Answer: \(156\).

examples.title: Find the integer in a factorial equation
examples.question: Find the non-negative integer \(r\) for which \(\frac{(r+2)!}{r!}=380\).
examples.solution:
Expand and cancel to obtain \((r+2)(r+1)=380\).

The two consecutive factors are \(19\) and \(20\). The other algebraic root is negative.

Answer: \(18\).

lessons.title: Arrangements in a row
lessons.summary: Count arrangements of distinct objects with position and adjacency restrictions.
lessons.objective: Count arrangements of distinct objects with position and adjacency restrictions.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to count arrangements of distinct objects with position and adjacency restrictions.
lessons.ideas:
Fill restricted positions first. The remaining places use the objects that remain.

A required adjacent group acts as one item when counting its position.

Count all arrangements, then subtract those where the pair is adjacent.
lessons.method:
If two named objects occupy both ends in either order, count both left–right choices and arrange the middle.

Count the internal arrangements separately and multiply. Put the distinct members back into their block after moving it.

The complement is useful because a single block count covers every forbidden adjacent position.
mistakes: Filling both end positions uses two objects. They cannot reappear in the middle.
Treating the pair as a block removes an outside position, not an internal order.
The words 'not together' describe the complement of the block count.

examples.title: Use the product rule to arrange distinct objects
examples.question: Distinct tiles are placed in a row. There are 12 objects. How many orders are possible with no restriction?
examples.solution:
There are 12 choices for the first place, 11 for the next, and so on down to one.

Multiply these choices to obtain \(12!\).

Answer: \(479001600\).

examples.title: Keep two positions adjacent
examples.question: Distinct books are placed on a shelf from left to right. There are 9 objects. The bird and tree books must be adjacent. How many orders are possible?
examples.solution:
Treat the two named objects as a block. Arrange this block and the 7 remaining objects.

Multiply \(8!\) by two because the order inside the block can be reversed.

Answer: \(80640\).

examples.title: Count only separated pairs
examples.question: Distinct radio jingles are scheduled in a list. There are 6 objects. The opening-theme and chime recordings must not be next to one another. How many orders are possible?
examples.solution:
All orders give \(6!\). The adjacent pair can be treated as one item, with two possible internal orders.

Subtract \(2\times 5!\) from the unrestricted count.

Answer: \(480\).

lessons.title: Permutations and ordered selections
lessons.summary: Choose and order a smaller set of distinct objects.
lessons.objective: Choose and order a smaller set of distinct objects.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to choose and order a smaller set of distinct objects.
lessons.ideas:
Use \({}^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\) for r different roles from n distinct items.

A candidate barred from the first slot may still be used later.

Place the required item in one available slot, then order the remaining choices.
lessons.method:
List the roles in a fixed sequence. The second selection has one fewer choice than the first.

Find the total and subtract the orders with that candidate first. Check each permitted later slot still has the right options.

A count for one possible position must be multiplied by the number of legal positions. All these cases are disjoint.
mistakes: A selection rule counts a set only once. It cannot distinguish first place from second place.
Removing a candidate from the pool entirely is a stronger restriction.
A required item is not necessarily fixed in the first slot.

examples.title: Count ordered selections
examples.question: A workshop has 15 distinct speaker applications. In how many ways can the organiser assign the 4 numbered speaking slots? A candidate or item may be used only once.

examples.title: Exclude one assignment to a slot
examples.question: A workshop has 10 distinct speaker applications. To assign the 5 numbered speaking slots, one particular candidate or item cannot fill the first slot but may fill another slot. How many results are possible?
examples.solution:
Count all results with \({}^{10}P_{5}\). There are \({}^{9}P_{4}\) results with the restricted item first.

Subtract the restricted results only. The restricted item is allowed in the other slots.

Answer: \(27216\).

examples.title: Include a specified item somewhere in an order
examples.question: A workshop has 15 distinct speaker applications. To assign the 5 numbered speaking slots, a named item or candidate must be used. How many results are possible?
examples.solution:
Choose one of the 5 positions for the specified item.

Order the remaining 4 positions in \({}^{14}P_{4}\) ways and multiply.

Answer: \(120120\).

lessons.title: Combinations and group quotas
lessons.summary: Count selections by group, using exact quotas and complements.
lessons.objective: Count selections by group, using exact quotas and complements.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to count selections by group, using exact quotas and complements.
lessons.ideas:
Use \(\binom nr=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}\) when the chosen objects form one set.

Pick the required number from each group and multiply.

For at least one, count all selections except those containing none of the required group.
lessons.method:
Decide whether a different order produces a different outcome. If the set is unchanged, divide the ordered count by the internal orders.

Use a row of group sizes above the row of numbers required. Check the required counts add to the size of the selection.

For two exact quotas, count each separately and add. For at least one, a single forbidden case may be quicker.
mistakes: Using an ordered formula counts the same selection several times.
The order of choices within each group has no effect.
At least one includes every allowed positive quota.

examples.title: Count unordered selections
examples.question: To make library sets, a curator may choose from 5 distinct biographies and 10 distinct novels. Selections of 4 items are unordered. How many different selections are possible with no further restriction?
examples.solution:
Choose 4 of the 15 distinct items. Use \(\binom{15}{4}\).

Divide the ordered count by \(4!\) to account for all the descriptions of the same set.

Answer: \(1365\).

examples.title: Meet an exact two-group quota
examples.question: To make library sets, a curator may choose from 10 distinct biographies and 10 distinct novels. Selections of 4 items are unordered. How many selections contain exactly 2 of the biographies?
examples.solution:
Choose 2 of the biographies, then 2 of the novels.

Both choices are needed, so multiply \(\binom{10}{2}\) by \(\binom{10}{2}\).

Answer: \(2025\).

examples.title: Require at least one from a group
examples.question: To make garden trials, a curator may choose from 7 distinct herbs and 11 distinct shrubs. Selections of 4 items are unordered. How many selections contain at least one of the herbs?
examples.solution:
All selections: \(\binom{18}{4}\). Those with none of the herbs: \(\binom{11}{4}\).

Discard just that single excluded class.

Answer: \(2730\).

lessons.title: Recovering an unknown count
lessons.summary: Translate a stated count into an equation and check the domain.
lessons.objective: Translate a stated count into an equation and check the domain.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to translate a stated count into an equation and check the domain.
lessons.ideas:
Two different labelled positions give n times one fewer than n.

Every unordered pair has two descriptions if you write its members in order.

Write adjacent combination counts as factorial quotients and cancel before evaluating.
lessons.method:
Use the two factors to build a quadratic. The number of people or objects is a positive whole number.

Divide by two, form the equation, multiply through, then solve for the positive integer.

The ratio of \(\binom n{r+1}\) to \(\binom nr\) is \(\frac{n-r}{r+1}\) where both are defined.
mistakes: The value of the smaller factor is the supply after the first choice.
An ordered pair count is double the number of two-element sets.
Preserve the order of the ratio. Reversing numerator and denominator reverses the result.

examples.title: Recover the group size from ordered pairs
examples.question: There are 702 ways to name a first and second person from a group of \(n\) distinct people. Determine \(n\).
examples.solution:
Use \(n(n-1)=702\).

The roots are \(27\) and \(-26\). Only the first is a possible group size.

Answer: \(27\).

examples.title: Recover the group size from pair counts
examples.question: A mixer organiser chooses two different people from a group of \(n\). There are 496 different unordered pairs. Determine \(n\).
examples.solution:
Set \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=496\).

The roots of the resulting quadratic are \(32\) and \(-31\). The group size must be positive.

Answer: \(32\).

examples.title: Compare successive combination counts
examples.question: Find the value of \(\frac{\binom{45}{2}}{\binom{45}{1}}\) in simplest form.
examples.solution:
Write both combinations using factorials. The common \(45!\) cancels.

The ratio reduces to \(\frac{44}{2}\).

Answer: \(22\).
